name: Macabeo

lines.s10: Macabeo is the quiet white grape of Cava and, as Viura, of white Rioja: green apple, pear and a note of almond.
lines.s20: Macabeo is a white grape of northern Spain, called Viura in Rioja, and it is one of the three grapes of Cava. It gives a fresh, gentle wine of green apple, pear and lemon, and a golden, nutty one after years in cask.
lines.s45: Macabeo is the grape behind two Spanish wines you know. It is one of the three grapes of Cava, from Catalonia, and in Rioja, as Viura, it leads the white wine. It tastes of green apple, pear and lemon, with a hint of almond. It is dry and fairly light, with gentle acidity. As Cava it gets its bubbles in the bottle, the way Champagne does, and the still wines are mostly made fresh in steel. Fried fish, cured ham and grilled vegetables all suit it. A few old cellars in Rioja still age it for years in cask, until it turns golden and tastes of hazelnut and beeswax.
lines.sale: Macabeo, as Cava, has bubbles made in the bottle as Champagne's are, and a dry, green apple freshness that suits almost any starter. It goes with anything salty or fried, and an aged white Rioja is worth keeping in mind for the roast chicken.

glass.lead: Green apple, pear and lemon with camomile and bitter almond, light and gentle; with cask age, hazelnut and beeswax.

ladder.where: Rioja Alta and the central basin of the Penedès
La Mancha, the coastal Penedès and Roussillon

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, gentler from warm sites, alcohol moderate, body light to medium; as Cava, a fine and steady sparkle.

home.home: Northern Spain. In Catalonia it is one of the three grapes of Cava, with Xarel·lo and Parellada, picked early and fermented a second time in the bottle. In Rioja, as Viura, it leads the white wines: mostly fresh from steel, and in the old style aged for years in cask until golden and nutty.
home.abroad: Across the Pyrenees, in Roussillon, it is Macabeu, a grape of the dry white blends and of the amber, fortified Rivesaltes. It is rarely grown outside Spain and the south of France.

service.temp: 43 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, as Cava; a cask aged white Rioja warmer.
service.glass: A tulip for Cava; a white wine glass for still wines, a wider bowl for cask aged Rioja.
service.decant: No for Cava. An old, cask aged white Rioja can open with a little air; taste first.
service.age: Cava and young whites within two or three years; cask aged white Rioja can keep ten years and more.

labels.means: The grape's name in Rioja, Navarra and Rueda.
Spanish sparkling wine made in the bottle, classically from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada.
White Rioja, led by Viura: fresh and young, or aged in oak as Crianza, Reserva or Gran Reserva.
The grape's Catalan and French name, in Roussillon's dry whites and in Rivesaltes.
Cava with under three grams of sugar a litre and none added: drier than Brut.

guest.a: It is made the same way, with the second fermentation in the bottle, but from Spanish grapes, Macabeo among them. It tends to taste of green apple and almond, a little softer than Champagne.

guest.q: The label says Viura. Is that Macabeo?
guest.a: Yes, the same grape. Rioja calls it Viura and Catalonia calls it Macabeo, so the still white of one region and the sparkling wine of the other share a grape.

guest.q: Why is this white Rioja so golden?
guest.a: It was aged for years in oak casks, the traditional way. Slow contact with air turns it gold and gives hazelnut, beeswax and honey. It is meant to taste like that; it is not spoiled.

compare.tell: Glera, as Prosecco, gets its bubbles in a tank and tastes of pear and acacia blossom, soft and often off dry; Macabeo, as Cava, is drier, with toast and almond.
Grenache Blanc is fuller, rounder and warmer on the finish; Macabeo, the Viura of Rioja, is lighter and leaner, with less alcohol.
Verdejo is louder and greener, with lime, fennel and a bitter finish; Macabeo is quieter and more neutral, with green apple and almond.

profile.st: Pale lemon, gold with cask age · Body light to medium · Acid medium · Alcohol moderate · Dry, still or sparkling
profile.fruit: Green apple, ripe pear, lemon zest; yellow apple from warm sites
profile.other: Camomile, acacia blossom and bitter almond; bread dough and toast as Cava; hazelnut, beeswax and honey after long cask ageing
profile.tell: A quiet, gentle white of green apple and almond: the freshness in a Cava blend, or the golden, nutty frame of an aged white Rioja
profile.regions: Catalonia (Cava and Penedès); Rioja, Navarra and Rueda as Viura; La Mancha; Roussillon as Macabeu
profile.confuse: Verdejo is greener and more bitter; Grenache Blanc is fuller and warmer; Glera, as Prosecco, is softer, with acacia blossom; Chardonnay is weightier, with butter or vanilla from the cellar

cards.front: Macabeo: what is it called in Rioja, and what does it do there?
cards.back: Viura. It is the main grape of white Rioja: fresh and neutral when young, golden, nutty and waxy after long ageing in oak.

cards.front: Which three grapes make the classic Cava blend, and what is Macabeo's part?
cards.back: Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Macabeo brings fruit and apple freshness. The wine ferments a second time in the bottle and rests at least nine months on its lees.

cards.front: Macabeo blind, as Cava: what parts it from Prosecco?
cards.back: Toast and almond from time on its lees in the bottle, and a drier finish. Prosecco, made in a tank from Glera, is softer, with pear and acacia blossom and no bready note.

questions.q: A guest who enjoyed a white Rioja labelled Viura asks which sparkling wine is made from the same grape. What do you bring?
questions.exp: Viura is Rioja's name for Macabeo, one of the three classic grapes of Cava with Xarel·lo and Parellada. Prosecco is made from Glera, and Franciacorta mostly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

questions.q: A blind white is deep gold and dry, with hazelnut, beeswax, honey and dried apple over bright acidity, the mark of years in old oak casks. Which wine is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Gold colour with hazelnut, beeswax and honey points to Viura aged for years in cask, the old style of white Rioja. Albariño and Verdejo are pale, fresh and usually unoaked.

questions.q: A guest asks how Cava gets its bubbles. What do you tell him?
opts: A second fermentation in the bottle
A second fermentation in a sealed tank
One fermentation finished in the bottle
questions.exp: Cava is made by the traditional method: a second fermentation in the bottle and at least nine months on its lees. The sealed tank is the method of Prosecco.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: northern Spain (Cava in Catalonia, Viura in Rioja), with Macabeu in Roussillon given as abroad.

A new grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the seven targets are Penedès, Rioja, Navarra, Rueda and Toro, La Mancha, Languedoc-Roussillon and Spain, each a page whose own record names Macabeo, Viura or Macabeu.

No Codex record is contradicted. The Codex already holds Viura as the backbone of white Rioja (neutral and fresh when young, nutty and waxy in the long oaked whites), Macabeo as one of the three grapes of Cava (fruit and apple freshness, early picked, gentle in acidity), the nine months on the lees, Brut Nature under three grams, and Macabeu in Roussillon's white blends and the ambré styles of Rivesaltes.
Acidity: the Codex and the Cava board call it gentle or moderate, while the Rioja council's sheet speaks of notable acidity. The entry says medium, gentler from warm sites.

Hazelnut, beeswax, honey and toffee in the cask aged wines stand on Foods and Wines from Spain and on the Codex's own nutty and waxy. Camomile stands on a tasting note on the Rioja council's site and is otherwise a taster's reading of the floral note both councils give; acacia blossom likewise.
The ladder is a taster's reading of what warmth does to the grape (Rioja Alta and the higher Penedès against La Mancha, the coast and Roussillon); no source read sets it out.

Left out: the first written mention of the grape in the Penedès (the Cava board's pages give 1617 in one place and 1785 in another), its late budding (one source, which a research paper on its ripening partly contradicts), and any claim about how it resists or suffers air.
The entry agrees with the tells already written from the other side by the Glera pilot (Cava drier, with toast and almond) and by Grenache Blanc and Verdejo (Macabeo lighter, leaner and quieter).

No dish from the Creole table is given: the oysters and the shrimp remoulade are already taken by the neighbours of this chunk, and nothing else on that table suits the grape better than fried fish and ham.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
